text: Overtime or a Second Job at $48 an Hour: Which Pays More?
Single hourly workers earning $32 an hour full time who could add 8 extra hours of work a week.
Work those 8 hours as overtime at $48 an hour, or at a second job paying $48 an hour?
We run the full federal tax math on both paths, including the new overtime break, and find what a side job must pay to match.
For a single worker paid $32 an hour (the typical production/nonsupervisory wage, $32.38 in June 2026, rounded) adding 400 hours a year, both paths pay $19,200 gross at $48 an hour.
Only the half-time premium, $6,400 (33.33% of the overtime pay), is deductible, and only from federal income tax; payroll tax of $1,468.80 applies either way.

Federal income tax on the extra pay is $2,816 as overtime versus $4,224 at a second job, so overtime keeps $14,915 versus $13,507: $1,408 more a year (total federal tax on the extra pay 22.32% vs 29.65%).
A second job would have to pay about $53.00 an hour to leave the same take-home as overtime at $48.
Hearing 'no tax on overtime', many hourly workers assume overtime pay is now tax-free (so a side job would have to pay far more to compete); others assume the tax treatment of the two is the same.
note: States beliefs, not results; the check confirms the result contradicts them (overtime still taxed, treatments differ, break-even is not far above the overtime rate).

text: Overtime does keep more, but the gap is a fixed, modest amount per hour (the premium times the bracket rate), not the whole overtime check: a side job paying a few dollars an hour more than the overtime rate leaves the same take-home.
note: "fixed, modest amount per hour" = ot_advantage_per_hour_usd = premium_per_hour_usd x marginal_bracket_pct; "a few dollars an hour more" = breakeven_markup_usd.

text: Under current law it ends after tax year 2028.
The wage is the national average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees for June 2026 (AHETPI via FRED), rounded to $32.
Only overtime required by federal law (over 40 hours a week) counts.
State-only daily overtime, double time beyond 1.5x, and union or employer premiums above the federal requirement do not qualify.
The side job is assumed to be W-2 work.
note: W-2 is a form name, not a quantity.

text: Self-employment (1099) work would add employer-side payroll tax and could qualify for other deductions, and the model does not cover it.
note: 1099 is a form name, not a quantity.

text: Tax year 2026, single filer, standard deduction ($16,100), no other income, no dependents or credits.
Regular job: 40 hours x 52 weeks at the regular rate; extra work: 8 hours a week for 50 weeks (400 hours).

Overtime is required by federal overtime law (over 40 hours in a workweek) at exactly 1.5 times the regular rate and reported by the employer as qualified overtime compensation; only the 0.5x premium is deductible.
